note: Hints only — no flags. Safe to feed to a solver when stuck.

targets.basic: User-controlled text is rendered into a privileged page without being escaped. A normal text node would be safe; some sink isn't.
targets.verbose: Profile fields stored at signup are surfaced verbatim in an admin listing. The admin renderer reaches for an HTML-injection escape hatch to bold the label rather than composing JSX. Anything an attacker writes into the field flows through unchanged. The exfiltration target is the admin's own session.

targets.basic: Some authed endpoints look up records by an URL-supplied id without checking the record belongs to the caller. Try changing the id.
targets.verbose: An order-detail handler accepts an integer id from the path and fetches by primary key alone. Ownership filtering exists in the list endpoint but was forgotten on the detail and the cancel handlers. Sequential integer ids make enumeration trivial.

targets.basic: Some routes are reserved for internal traffic only. The edge is supposed to strip the trust marker from public callers — but the strip list isn't exhaustive.
targets.verbose: An internal-traffic header is honored on a reserved API prefix. The reverse proxy strips a couple of internal headers on inbound, but this one was added after the strip rules were last updated. Pair with a forged or leaked admin token to reach handlers that expect either real auth or the internal marker.

targets.basic: A legacy verifier accepts tokens whose signing claim is more permissive than it should be. Some recognized algorithms shouldn't be acceptable at all.
targets.verbose: Mobile v1 compatibility left an unsigned-token branch in the legacy JWT verifier. Mint a token whose header advertises an algorithm that does not require a secret, set the claims you want, and submit it to a legacy endpoint that falls back to the v1 verifier.

targets.basic: A legacy code path is meant to be configured at deploy time but has a fallback. Find the fallback value; it's the secret.
targets.verbose: Dev-environment convenience defaults sometimes get committed to the schema's env parser. A legacy v1 verifier reaches for an env var whose default value is a recognizable placeholder. Mint a token with the missing-kid path and sign with that placeholder.

targets.basic: A reset token is generated from inputs an outside observer can reasonably predict. Knowing the inputs is the same as knowing the token.
targets.verbose: The reset-link token reduces to a short prefix of a hash over the user id and the current epoch milliseconds. Both are observable or guessable in a tight window. Brute the few seconds around the request to find a token that the reset endpoint accepts.

targets.basic: An admin search endpoint has a "perf mode" toggle. Behind it, the query builder takes a shortcut that puts user input directly into SQL.
targets.verbose: Flipping the perf query parameter swaps the parameterized search for a raw concatenation of the search term into a LIKE clause. Standard string-quote-and-close payloads work. The endpoint is admin-only, so you'll need either a forged token or a chained bypass to reach it.

targets.basic: A value you control at rest is later concatenated into a raw query somewhere else. The write path is safe; a downstream read is not.
targets.verbose: A profile field you set through the normal (parameterized, safe) update is stored verbatim. An admin-only compliance report later iterates active cases and splices that stored value into a raw, unparameterized similarity query. Because the dangerous read is far from the safe write, this is a second-order injection. Time-based blind techniques work; the sink runs server-side under the admin's request.

targets.basic: A "preserve the user's destination" pattern accepts a value that isn't validated against same-origin. Protocol-relative URLs slip.
targets.verbose: The login flow reads a query parameter and hands it straight to the client router after auth. There's no allow-list check for a leading slash or for protocol-relative shapes. Phish-friendly when paired with a clone of the login screen.

targets.basic: A user-named file is joined into a server-controlled directory without normalization. Going up the tree leaves the safe area.
targets.verbose: The KYC document fetcher takes a filename, joins it under the uploads directory, and reads the result. No canonical-path check blocks `..` segments. The lab plants a marker file outside the uploads area to confirm a successful traversal.

targets.basic: A pinned dependency in the manifest carries a known security advisory. Run a dep audit and you'll see it; look the advisory up to learn what it allows.
targets.verbose: The compliance importer parses XML with an older release of a library whose default options accept a specific prototype-naming child. The advisory ID itself is the secret here. Find the audit finding, name it, submit it as the discovered material.

targets.basic: An admin export feature shells out to a helper tool. A request parameter lands in the command string with no escaping.
targets.verbose: The compliance PDF export builds a single command string and runs it through a shell instead of passing an argument array. A query parameter for the output name is concatenated in directly. With shell parsing in play, metacharacters let you chain a second command before the output redirect. Observe success out-of-band — a measurable delay is enough; the helper tool itself need not even be present.

targets.basic: A markdown sanitizer is meant to strip script-loading attributes. Its pattern is narrower than the set of inputs an HTML parser will accept.
targets.verbose: The admin-side ticket renderer pipes message bodies through a sanitizer whose handler-stripping regex assumes one specific quote style. Authoring the body with the OTHER quote style on a handler attribute slips through. The rendered HTML lands inside an admin-only page rendered with dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

targets.basic: A verifier picks the key by name and trusts whatever the token says about how to use it. Same lookup feeds both symmetric and asymmetric paths.
targets.verbose: The legacy verifier loads a kid-named key file and hands the bytes to whichever crypto path the JWT header asks for. Public-key material is exposed via JWKS; sign an HMAC token using those bytes as the secret and the verifier will accept it.

targets.basic: A token header field names which key to verify with. That name is turned into a file lookup without restriction.
targets.verbose: The legacy verifier treats the token's key-id header as a filesystem location and reads whatever it points at, using the bytes as the HMAC secret. A traversal sequence in the key-id reaches a process-readable file whose contents you can predict; sign your token with those bytes as the secret and the legacy verify path accepts it. Whitelisting the key-id would have stopped this.

targets.basic: Refresh tokens are meant to rotate, but the old one is never invalidated when a new pair is issued. A captured token keeps working.
targets.verbose: Each refresh call mints a new access/refresh pair but never marks the presented refresh token consumed — there is no used-at or revoked-at state on the record. A token captured by any means keeps minting access tokens for its full multi-week lifetime, even after the legitimate user has refreshed. Confirm by replaying the same refresh body repeatedly and watching it keep succeeding.

targets.basic: A form-driven update treats every submitted field as authoritative. Adding fields the form never advertised changes them anyway.
targets.verbose: A Server Action receives FormData on the server, iterates the entries, and forwards them into a Prisma update without an explicit allow-list. Fields like fee tier and order status get set from any key the caller chooses. There's no ownership check either.

targets.basic: The WebSocket gateway does not validate where the upgrade request came from. Anything that can establish the connection can subscribe.
targets.verbose: The upgrade handler reads the access token from the query string and never checks the Origin header. A cross-origin page can open the socket with the victim's cookie-resident token. Once connected there's also no allow-list on the channel name passed to the subscribe message.

targets.basic: The address validator is too forgiving. It accepts networks it should not, silently cleans some characters, and skips a checksum.
targets.verbose: One permissive validator covers mainnet, testnet, and regtest prefixes, strips zero-width Unicode before checking, and never verifies the bech32 checksum. The zero-width strip is the sharpest edge: a string that displays as a victim address to a reviewer normalizes server-side to an attacker address once the invisible characters are removed. Submit such an address where a withdrawal destination is validated.

targets.basic: The matching engine doesn't refuse to cross orders that share the same owner. Trades against yourself print to the public feed.
targets.verbose: Spot up a resting limit at a chosen price, then immediately fire a matching order from the same account. A real trade row writes; the public last-price feed updates. Downstream consumers — like the margin liquidation watcher — read the contaminated price.

targets.basic: Daily withdrawal limits use a calendar-day bucket. The boundary between buckets is a wall-clock moment; two transactions on opposite sides of it both pass.
targets.verbose: The limit ledger keys on userId, asset, and a UTC-truncated date. A withdrawal at 23:59:59 and another at 00:00:01 the next day are scored against different buckets even though they're seconds apart. Stage a tier-1 account near the boundary, drain the bucket, flip the date, drain again.

targets.basic: A tier check compares values whose types may differ. JavaScript's comparison rules sometimes pick a sort order you don't expect.
targets.verbose: requireTier accepts either a number or a string for the tier operands and runs a less-than comparison. When one side is a string and the other is a number, the comparison stringifies and some larger tier numbers compare LESS than smaller ones. Submit the string form to bypass the gate.

targets.basic: The balance check and the debit are not in one transaction. Fire two requests at once and both see the same funds.
targets.verbose: Submitting a withdrawal reads available balance, checks a limit, then debits — none of it inside a single transaction. Two near-simultaneous requests both read the same balance before either writes, so both pass and both debit. Widen the window with parallel, tightly-timed requests (single-packet style). The fix would be a conditional debit guarded by an available-greater-or-equal predicate, or a serializable transaction.

targets.basic: There is a money-movement path that is not a withdrawal, so it skips the withdrawal daily-limit and tier checks entirely.
targets.verbose: Internal account-to-account transfers debit the sender and credit the recipient but never touch the withdrawal limit ledger, and the route enforces only the lowest tier floor. Relay value to a second (or colluding) account that then withdraws through its own untouched daily quota. Net effect: a low-tier user moves far more than their stated daily limit off-platform by hopping accounts.

targets.basic: A cancel handler and a concurrent fill don't share a transaction. Two passes through the path can produce more refund than the original lock.
targets.verbose: The order cancel decrements locked balance and increments available based on a snapshot read taken outside the database transaction. A concurrent partial fill that completes between the read and the write makes the refund larger than what was actually locked. Race the cancel against a small market order on a quiet pair.

targets.basic: Two pieces of code parse the same signed payload differently. Validation reads one part; broadcast reads another.
targets.verbose: A treasury draft is validated against its intended outputs, then handed to the node to finalize — but the validator reads the first envelope segment while the finalize step canonicalizes to the last segment. Craft a payload with two segments: the first carrying the expected, benign output to pass validation, the last carrying your output to be broadcast. The two parsers disagree only on multi-segment inputs nobody tested.

targets.basic: A hand-rolled deep-merge walks attacker-supplied keys into a shared base object. A later reader inherits the polluted property and serves it.
targets.verbose: An internal trade-debug replay deep-merges your config into defaults without rejecting dangerous keys. A top-level pollution attempt is stripped by the schema, but a NESTED envelope survives and the merge walks into the prototype. A feature-flag resolver then iterates with a prototype-chain-walking loop, so the polluted property surfaces as an own key and serializes back, flipping an admin flag for a non-admin. Reach the replay route through the internal-trace bypass first.

targets.basic: An auth middleware short-circuits when it sees a particular request header — one the client can simply send.
targets.verbose: An early branch in the framework middleware returns immediately when a subrequest-marker header is present, meant to let internal probes skip auth. The header is attacker-suppliable, so sending any non-empty value skips the role check ahead of admin handlers. Those handlers then trust a client-sent user-id header. This mirrors a known framework middleware-bypass CVE-2025-29927. Use it to list the user table or mint admin users.

targets.basic: An endpoint fetches an attacker-supplied URL with only the most obvious local addresses on the deny list. Non-loopback internal hosts get through.
targets.verbose: The KYC URL-import flow checks for a tiny set of loopback host strings before fetching. Cloud-metadata aliases, RFC1918 ranges, and internal docker-network names aren't on the list. The result is reachable to the trainee in the returned document body.

targets.basic: KYC document upload trusts the uploaded mime type when the client hides the real one. Same-origin rendering picks up the trusted mime.
targets.verbose: When the client sends a generic application/octet-stream, the server infers the mime from the filename's extension. A polyglot file that begins with image bytes but whose name ends in .html is served back with the html mime, inside an iframe whose blob URL shares the same origin. The admin viewer is the sink.

targets.basic: Top-tier deposits are credited at zero confirmations. If the transaction is later replaced and dropped, the credit is not reversed.
targets.verbose: A premium tier maps to zero required confirmations, so the deposit worker credits balance the moment a transaction appears in the mempool. Replace-by-fee the transaction so the original drops; the worker marks the deposit dropped but never debits the balance it already credited — there is no reconciliation. Reach the tier (legitimately or via an admin path), self-send a deposit, drop it, repeat. Balance grows with no on-chain settlement.

targets.basic: Trading-volume for fee tiers counts fills it should not. One side's cancelled orders still accrue toward the discount.
targets.verbose: The fee-tier volume query filters out cancelled taker orders but forgets the maker side, so a filled-then-cancelled maker order still counts toward 30-day volume. Pair with self-trading: place a maker order, fill it from a second account, cancel the maker, and the trade row survives to inflate volume. A few hundred wash cycles reach a top fee tier at near-zero real cost.

targets.basic: Interest is computed for the elapsed window, then split across whoever is supplying right now — including someone who only just joined.
targets.verbose: The accrual worker computes interest from the borrow side across the whole window, but reads the supplier set AFTER and divides by current supply. Deposit a large amount into a high-utilization pool just before the periodic tick and you capture a share of yield earned while your capital was not at risk. Withdraw right after the tick. The pool's rate and last-accrual timing are inferable from public data, so you can front-run the tick.

targets.basic: A reward-claim endpoint reads unclaimed rows then marks them claimed, but not atomically. Fire it twice at once to claim twice.
targets.verbose: Claiming staking rewards reads the not-yet-claimed rows, then updates them to claimed with no transaction and no claimed-is-null guard on the write. Two simultaneous claims for the same position both observe the same unclaimed set before either write lands, so each credits the full reward. Net N-times payout for N parallel requests. An atomic conditional update, or a serializable transaction, would close it.

targets.basic: An internal-console header is honored by a public endpoint. The edge strips some internal headers but not all of them.
targets.verbose: The OTC accept handler reads a header that names the caller's desk role and applies the corresponding fee tier directly. The reverse proxy strips the user-id header on inbound but the desk-role header was added after the strip list was last updated.

targets.basic: When a withdrawal's fee is bumped down, the difference is refunded immediately — before the replacement transaction is known to confirm.
targets.verbose: Bumping a broadcast withdrawal to a lower fee synchronously credits the fee difference back to available balance, with no watcher to claw it back if the replacement is dropped from the mempool. A low replacement fee that never confirms (or gets dropped by a follow-on bump) leaves the user holding the refund and possibly the original settlement. Looping low-fee bumps across many withdrawals drains the books slowly without any single anomaly.

targets.basic: A secret was committed once and removed in a later commit. It is gone from the current tree but lives in history forever.
targets.verbose: An operational backup file was added in one commit and deleted in the next during a hotfix. The current checkout is clean, but the deleted blob — including a signing secret — remains in history. Scan all of history for the deleted file, or grep across past diffs for the secret name. The recovered value still matches the running stack's signing secret, so it forges accepted admin tokens. The discovered secret is itself the answer you submit.

targets.basic: A private-scope dependency is referenced without telling the package manager where to find it. The public registry is the fallback.
targets.verbose: The web app declares an optional dependency under a private scope. No registry-scope pin exists. An attacker who registers a package with the same name on the public registry can ship code that the install path would pull in. The scope is the secret you need to find in the manifest.

targets.basic: The edge and the app disagree on request framing. Both a length header and a chunked header get through, and the app is told to tolerate it.
targets.verbose: Two halves make this work: the reverse proxy forwards both a content-length and a chunked transfer-encoding header to the upstream, and the app process runs with a lenient HTTP parser that accepts the ambiguity instead of rejecting it. Send one request carrying both headers; the upstream desyncs on the chunked terminator and reads trailing bytes as a second request on the connection. Smuggle a privileged self-update onto a legitimate user's session. Finding only the proxy directives leaves you stuck until you also spot the parser flag.

targets.basic: A self-update endpoint accepts every column the validator declared optional. Some of those columns are not supposed to be user-mutable.
targets.verbose: The self-update handler defines a zod schema that lists optional role, kycTier, and feeTier fields, then forwards the validated body verbatim to a Prisma update on the caller's own row. Submitting any of those keys promotes the caller.

steps.basic: Recon. The signing material the running stack accepts may not live in HEAD.
steps.verbose: Operational backup files sometimes survive in version control after a delete. The leaked value should match a literal env variable that the deployed stack consumes.

steps.basic: Privilege bridge. Some internal-only headers escape the edge's strip list.
steps.verbose: Internal-traffic markers admit requests past auth on a reserved path prefix. Audit the proxy's strip rules for omissions; a single missing line is enough.

steps.basic: Asset move. Validation and broadcast may disagree on which segment of a payload is canonical.
steps.verbose: When a transaction draft includes more than one envelope segment, the validator and the node may pick different ones. The mismatch is the broadcasting primitive.

steps.basic: Edge framing. The reverse proxy tolerates ambiguous request framing.
steps.verbose: When a request carries both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, the proxy and the upstream may disagree on where one request ends and the next begins. Audit the proxy's framing directives.

steps.basic: Upstream parsing. Modern Node rejects framing ambiguity by default — unless told not to.
steps.verbose: A runtime option on the upstream relaxes the strict HTTP parser. Find the env or command-line flag that turns that strictness off, and confirm both edges and upstream agree.

steps.basic: Privilege write. A self-update endpoint accepts more fields than the form ever advertised.
steps.verbose: Smuggle a self-update request including a role field into a legitimate user's pipelined connection. The mass-assign on the receiving handler persists the change.

steps.basic: Self-matching. The engine doesn't refuse to cross orders that share an owner.
steps.verbose: Place a resting limit at a chosen price, then immediately fire a matching order from the same account. A real trade prints and the public last-price feed updates.

steps.basic: Oracle consumer. Some risk subsystem reads that public price.
steps.verbose: The margin liquidation watcher consumes the public last-price as its mark — no separate oracle, no median. Repeat the self-trade move to walk the mark in your direction.

steps.basic: Settlement. Liquidation rebates pay the keeper that claims them.
steps.verbose: Register as a keeper, watch the liquidation queue fire against the contaminated mark, and claim the rebate. The victim's position closes against synthetic price.

steps.basic: URL fetcher. Some endpoint pulls user-supplied URLs without a tight allow-list.
steps.verbose: A KYC import flow takes a URL and fetches it server-side. The reject list only blocks loopback strings; internal docker-network aliases get through.

steps.basic: Internal target. There's a service in the cluster that hands out short-lived credentials.
steps.verbose: A mock metadata service emits an IAM-style credential payload on a well-known path. The SSRF reaches it through the docker network alias; the credential body lands in the trainee's import response.

steps.basic: Storage retrieval. The credentials authenticate against a synthetic document store.
steps.verbose: A mock S3-style service trusts the metadata credentials and serves a KYC bucket listing under a predictable prefix. The bucket contains synthetic identity documents.
